cues.text: A Disputed Patriarch

In 858, the Byzantine emperor Michael III deposed the legitimate Patriarch of Constantinople, St. Ignatius , and installed in his place a brilliant layman, Photius , hastily ordained through all the clerical grades in a matter of days.
Ignatius refused to resign his office, and Pope St. Nicholas I , after examining the case, declined to recognize Photius, setting Rome and Constantinople on a collision course.
Photius responded by convening his own council in 867.
The council declared Nicholas deposed and excommunicated—an extraordinary breach that briefly severed communion between Christendom’s two great sees.
It left lasting resentments that would resurface in the definitive East-West Schism two centuries later.
A Change of Emperor
Later in 867, the usurper Basil I seized the Byzantine throne and, seeking reconciliation with Rome, deposed Photius and restored Ignatius to the patriarchate.
Both the new emperor and the restored patriarch petitioned Pope Adrian II , Nicholas's successor, for a general council to settle the affair once and for all.
Adrian sent three legates to preside in his name, and the council opened in the Hagia Sophia on October 5, 869 .
Attendance was thin at first — barely a dozen bishops at the opening session — a reflection of how much support Photius still commanded among the Byzantine clergy despite his removal.
The Condemnation of Photius
Over ten sessions, the council examined the acts of Photius's rival 867 council and formally burned them.
It renewed the earlier Roman excommunication of Photius and required attending bishops to sign a profession, the Libellus Satisfactionis , affirming Roman primacy and rejecting Photius's claims.
Photius himself, summoned before the assembly, refused to defend himself or renounce his position and was banished to a monastery.

By the tenth and final session, held on February 28, 870 in the presence of the emperor, attendance had grown to roughly 102 bishops, along with envoys from the Bulgarian king and the Western emperor Louis II.
The council's twenty-seven canons addressed the Photian affair directly and also renewed earlier condemnations of the last vestiges of iconoclasm and of lay interference in church governance.
A Council Later Disputed
The council's peace proved short-lived.
Ignatius died in 877, and Photius, restored to imperial favor, returned to the patriarchate.
A further council held in Constantinople in 879–880, attended by far more bishops, effectively reversed much of what had been decided in 869–870.
The Eastern Church came to regard that later, pro-Photian gathering — not this one — as authoritative.
As a result, the Catholic Church counts the 869–870 council as the eighth ecumenical council.
The Eastern Orthodox Church does not recognize it as ecumenical at all, considering the seven councils from Nicaea I through Nicaea II to be the complete and closed list.
This divergence in numbering is itself a small but telling symptom of the deepening estrangement between Rome and Constantinople in the decades before the definitive schism of 1054.
Legacy

Fourth Constantinople stands as the last ecumenical council held in the Christian East before the Great Schism, and its immediate resolution of the Photian affair proved far less durable than its framers hoped.
Its lasting historical significance lies less in any new doctrine — it defined none — than in what it reveals about the widening cultural and ecclesiastical gap between the Greek East and Latin West.

Disputes over a single disputed patriarch could no longer be settled to the lasting satisfaction of both halves of Christendom, a warning sign of the permanent rupture still a century and a half away.
